beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi Jeedigunta. This video is about a database update in the same regulatory pipeline from last week — one that could mark high-priority alerts 'emailed' even when no email had actually gone out for them — and the fix that scoped it to only what was actually sent.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: In that same pipeline, I found a step whose only job is to record 'this got emailed' — and it was using its own copy of the rule for what counts as high-priority, instead of checking what the email step had actually sent.
beats.new_visual_element: The 'Mark email sent' node, isolated, with a question mark over its condition

shot.note: Node box for 'Mark email sent' with a '?' over its WHERE condition.

beats.narration_text: The alert path is simple: insert the item, filter for anything with an urgency score above six, build an email from exactly those rows, send it, then mark those rows sent. Two steps decide what 'high priority' means here — and they were supposed to agree.
beats.new_visual_element: Two condition boxes side by side: urgency_score > 6 (High Priority Filter) vs. the old urgency_score > 7 OR impact_level IN ('Critical','High') (Mark email sent)

shot.note: [Source: A7-VERIFICATION.md 'The bug' section] Both conditions must be legible on screen simultaneously, not sequential cuts — see BEAT-SHEET.md's Legibility Contract.

beats.narration_text: Here's why they didn't agree. The scoring node sets impact level from the score — except for one shortcut: if the text matches an enforcement or fraud keyword, it jumps straight to High or Critical, no matter how low the score is. So an item scoring five or six can still read 'Critical' — low enough that the email filter would never pick it up, but high enough that the old update would still flip it to 'sent.'
beats.new_visual_element: The determineImpactLevel() function, the isEnforcement/isFraud bypass line highlighted

shot.note: [Source: A7-VERIFICATION.md 'Why the two rules disagree'] Highlight the bypass line in the same color as the mismatch arrows from B03 for visual continuity.

beats.narration_text: I queried the live table for exactly that mismatch. Twelve real rows, as of this week — including an actual SEC enforcement action, 'SEC Charges 21 Individuals With Alleged Wide-Reaching Insider Trading Scheme' — that the email filter would never select, but that the old query would have silently marked sent the next time it ran.
beats.new_visual_element: Query on screen, result count '12', one example row (id 153) shown with its title, urgency_score (5), and impact_level (Critical)

shot.note: [Source: A7-VERIFICATION.md 'Live measurement (2026-08-30)', re-verified live at build time 2026-08-30 21:04 — see SOURCES.md] FACTCHECK-approved conditional framing: 'would have,' never 'were.' Do not imply all 12 rows are equally significant — name only row 153.

beats.narration_text: The fix: stop re-deriving the rule. Read the exact ids the email step already produced, and only mark those sent.
beats.new_visual_element: Before/after SQL sitting together: old blanket WHERE clause vs. new WHERE id = ANY($1::int[]), id source (High Priority Filter node) annotated

shot.note: [Source: A7-VERIFICATION.md 'Fix'; commit 03ad1e0 in mycroft] Full before AND after query visible together, per the Legibility Contract.

beats.narration_text: A step that copies someone else's rule instead of reading their output isn't wrong today. It's wrong the day the two drift apart — and by then nothing threw an error to tell you.
